Accents on a Non-Final Atom of a Compound

Maqaf marks join two or more atoms into a single chanted word. In the prose system a chanted word usually has exactly one accent, and only in a small minority of cases two. Of the 36,786 maqaf compounds in the prose verses of MAM, 233 (0.63%) have an accent on a non-final atom. In every one of them the two accents sit on two atoms of the compound and never both on one, the compound itself having two atoms, or occasionally three. This page counts those cases, sorts them, and asks what they mean for one printed page in particular.

The motivation for this study is the chanted word

ל֣א־תעש֣ה

in Koren's Deuteronomy appendix Decalogue (the עליון) — one maqaf compound, with a munaḥ on both of its atoms. The Wikisource strand Koren otherwise follows in every accent has

ל֣א תעש֣ה

instead: two chanted words, each with a munaḥ of its own. Is there anything in Tanakh like it?

There is not. No maqaf compound in MAM's prose verses has the same accent on both atoms, not once. Nearly all of the 233 prose cases are a single grammatical category, a qadma before a zaqef qatan; and the one case whose non-final atom has a munaḥ is Isaiah 40:7

נ֣בל־צ֔יץ

which is not Koren's pair of accents either. Nor is any printed edition known to have Koren's compound before it.

What is counted

A maqaf joins an atom to the next, and what it makes is one chanted word. The question put to every maqaf compound in the Tanakh is whether an atom the maqaf joins has an accent of its own, over and above the accent the compound has on its last atom. A compound counts once however many of its atoms are accented, and it is counted against every maqaf compound in those verses, accented on one atom or on two.

A meteg and a silluq are one and the same sign. That sign counts here as an accent only on the last chanted word of a verse, where it is a silluq; anywhere else it is a meteg, which is not an accent at all.

Which text this page counts

Every count on this page is MAM's. MAM is a consensus text rather than a diplomatic one: not a single manuscript's reading, but the accentuation the Masoretic tradition converges on. It largely follows Breuer, but it is not one of Breuer's own editions.

The prose verses

A mark on a non-final atom is there because the compound is one chanted word, and a mark belonging to that chanted word as a whole has landed short of its last atom. The marks that can do this are a closed list, which Yeivin gives for the prose system: qadma before a zaqef qatan (metigah-zaqef, §224), munaḥ before a zaqef qatan (§221), a secondary merkha in the chanted word of a tipeḥa, of a silluq or of a tevir (§§233, 241), a secondary mahapakh in the chanted word of a tevir (§241), and the mayela tipeḥa before an etnaḥta or a silluq.

Of MAM's 233 cases, 230 are marks that are not the atom's own accent — all but one of them under a named category from that list — and three are undecided, their non-final atom never standing free elsewhere in the text for its mark's position to be checked. Deciding one is a matter of position, and needs no phonology: the atom is looked up elsewhere standing free, a chanted word by itself with an accent of its own, and the letters following the accent are counted in each. Judges 7:13 והנה־איש has its qadma two letters from the end, where among the 254 free-standing והנה the accent's usual place is one letter from the end — so the mark is not that atom's own accent, and it is the metigah of §224.

The cases, by configuration:

  • metigah-zaqef: a qadma before a zaqef qatan (§224) — 211
  • the mayela tipeḥa before an etnaḥta — 8
  • a secondary merkha in the silluq's chanted word (§233) — 4
  • a secondary merkha in the tipeḥa's chanted word (§233) — 4
  • the mayela tipeḥa before a silluq — 1
  • a munaḥ before a zaqef qatan (§221) — 1
  • no named configuration: the mark is simply not at that atom's own accent position — 1

Things are less tidy in a manuscript. Yeivin (§§293, 357) reports that some manuscripts have a maqaf even after an atom that keeps its own conjunctive, with no grammatical trigger at all, and names the Leningrad Codex for the habit. MAM, which is not a manuscript, has no case of it.

Koren's compound

Every one of those cases pairs two different accents: the compound's accent, and a secondary mark of a kind that can precede it. Koren's two are the same accent twice, and no chanted word in MAM is accented that way — so there is no category Koren's compound could be said to be following, and nothing in MAM it could be said to be repeating.

The Decalogue's Exodus 20:10 לא־תעשה has a munaḥ on each atom, but that is the two strands tangled together rather than either one of them: untangled, MAM's טעם עליון has no maqaf, and לא and תעשה are two chanted words, each with a munaḥ of its own — the very two atoms Koren has as one maqaf compound.

The nearest thing in a printed edition

None of the printed editions transcribed for these pages has the shape either. The nearest is the Simanim Tiqqun's munaḥ on the joined לא of לא־יהיה and of לא־תעשה — the same phenomenon, a non-final atom keeping its accent, one step short of the same shape, and in this very passage.

The poetic verses

The poetic system is a different matter, and different enough that the same count would not mean the same thing there. It puts two marks on one chanted word readily and systematically (Breuer, Chapter 9 §§20–26), where the prose system does so rarely and only within the closed list above. And many of its maqafs are not written at all: Breuer (§§27, 37) records that in poetic verses the maqaf after a secondary mark is customarily left unwritten while the atom still counts as joined, so a survey that finds compounds by looking for a written maqaf reaches only part of what is there. MAM's poetic verses have 17 cases by that measure, and MAM has the other part of the measure too: it supplies 116 gray maqafs, its own mark for a maqaf the manuscript leaves unwritten where the chanted word needs one. Of those, 69 join an atom that has an accent alongside the compound's accent; the other 47 have one accent written across the two atoms. Neither figure belongs beside the prose one.
